chapter: Regional bands, politics and travel abroad
title: Politics: Ben Davis, Paul Robeson and paid rallies
summary: Wilson explains his role on the entertainment committee for Ben Davis, a Robeson birthday show and a Republican rally, saying he was paid and never joined the left.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: (Inaudible) during the war when you had a problem. What was that problem about you down in the Village? There seemed to be some problem that you were in the wrong company, or something. And there was always some kind of problem that you could never -- now, I never got into this because I was with Cab Calloway and I never heard much there. Politically or something?

Oh, yeah. I was involved in the entertainment committee to promote the campaigns of Ben Davis. Adam Powell was leaving the -- he was the first Negro councilman in New York and he was leaving the council to go to Congress, to be a Congressman. And he threw his support behind Ben Davis who was a popular figure in Harlem. Because see, many Negros who were popular with the public, some of them -- not many but some went over on the left side, like Paul Robeson. Paul Robeson -- people worshipped Paul Robeson and Ben Davis was a tremendous figure. Ben Davis was one of the lawyers in the Scottsboro Case which was one of the most
famous cases of racial injustice in the 1930's. And he got famous that way and --

... he began to believe in Communism; the Communist movement liked Paul Robeson. So I was on the entertainment committee and went to a rally for Ben Davis, to get people to go out and vote for Ben Davis, and then I played for Paul Robeson's birthday part; a big birthday party at the Armory or somewhere like that, along with a lot of entertainers.
But I would do that -- I didn't care about Paul Robeson's politics. And, and, then, too, I got paid -- I got paid, too. Musicians, we can't go around politicking and not getting paid, so we got paid.
That's right.
And I played for a Republican rally in Chicago. Got paid -- and Roscoe Simmons was the speaker, do you remember him?
Surely; yes, indeed.

The man who gave the nominating address for Hoover at the Republican convention. I played a Republican rally where Roscoe Simmons spellbinded those to diverge a little bit, he could talk like Adam Powell; he could spellbind the public people -- Roscoe could talk, but after he finished, nobody could remember a thing he said, but while he was saying it, it was fascinating to hear!
That's great.
And a lot of movie stars got involved with things
like that, too.
Oh, sure.
It was mostly at coffees or something like that.

But see, I've never felt anything from that -- maybe, I don't know if it hurt my career, as I have always done well financially, but as far as I know, it didn't mean a penny to me. But I never did join up with that leftist movement. I would bother to find out, though; I would talk a lot to people who were in it. I talked to some teachers to find out just what it was all about.
